title: Linear, Mobius, polynomial, Fourier and Laplace maps: each has one failure that the figure is built to show
summary: These course animations take a classical transformation and put its characteristic failure on screen: transient growth hidden by eigenvalues, circles-to-circles of a Mobius map, Runge's blow-up of equispaced polynomials, aliasing of a fast sinusoid, and the pole positions that decide a decaying response. Companion static figures show a nilpotent shear flow, Mobius classes, a Runge comparison, a 21 and 11 Hz alias, and the resolvent gain of a non-normal matrix.

media.alt: Four stills in a grid. A unit circle stretched into thin ellipses by the matrix exponential with a norm curve that rises before it decays; a plane with three circles and two stars beside the same picture on a sphere; a degree 32 interpolant that oscillates wildly at the ends against a smooth one; a fast sampled sinusoid with a slower dashed alias and a single spike in its frequency spectrum.

read_the_figure.question: What does this classical transform promise, and which printed number tells me where the promise breaks?
read_the_figure.axes: S010 left: the image of the unit circle under exp(tA); right: norm against time on a log axis. S011: plane (left) and sphere view (right). S012: the interpolant on [-1, 1], and maximum error against degree n on a log axis. S013: time (0 to 1 s) and DFT bin in hertz. S014: the complex s-plane and the impulse response against time.
look_at: S010: the solid curve is the 2-norm of exp(tA); the dashed line is the decay the eigenvalues promise, exp(-t). The norm rises first (to about 2.5 near t = 0.7) before falling.

S011: three circles in the plane map to circles or lines under a Mobius map; the title carries the trace (1.33, elliptic) and the sphere view reports a plane-fit residual (3e-16) and a Cauchy-Riemann drift (2e-16).
S012: the orange curve is equispaced interpolation, the blue is Chebyshev; the title states their maximum errors, 5.1e+03 against 1.4e-03 at degree 32.
S013: grey is the true 17 Hz wave, red dots the samples, dashed blue the 15 Hz alias that fits the same samples; the spectrum's peak is in bin 15, not 17.
S014: crosses are poles; the shaded region is where the transform converges (Re s > -1.83); the right panel shows the impulse response that the pole positions imply.
Companion figures. Shear as a flow: the matrix [[0, 2], [0, 0]] has both eigenvalues zero, yet the norm grows linearly in time (dotted lines k y2(0) t), not exponentially.

Mobius circles and lines: a family of concentric circles and a grid of lines mapped to circles and lines; the four Mobius classes (elliptic, hyperbolic, parabolic, loxodromic) show different orbit patterns of the iteration z to f(z), each with a fixed point marked by a cross.

Runge companion: equispaced interpolation oscillates to values near -60 at the ends of the interval while Chebyshev interpolation is indistinguishable from the target; the residual panel says the same.
Aliasing companion: a 21 Hz and an 11 Hz sinusoid share the same samples (sampling at 32 Hz).
Resolvent gain: the 2-norm of the resolvent against angular frequency for a non-normal matrix is about five times that of a normal matrix with the same eigenvalues at low frequency.
read_the_figure.proves: Each figure turns a theorem into a witness: eigenvalues do not control short-time growth of a non-normal matrix; Mobius maps preserve circles and angles to round-off; node placement decides whether interpolation converges; sampling below twice the frequency makes two sinusoids indistinguishable; poles in the left half-plane mean a decaying response.
if_wrong: A norm curve that rises above 1 although all eigenvalues are negative: the matrix is non-normal, and eigenvalues alone say nothing about the first moments.
A residual far above 1e-15 on the Mobius checks: the map was composed or discretized incorrectly.
Errors that grow with degree: the interpolation nodes, not the function, are the problem.
A spectrum peak at a lower frequency than the signal: aliasing, so the sampling rate is too low.
A pole with positive real part: the response grows, however well the fit looks over a short window.
must_check: Which norm is plotted, and whether the eigenvalue bound is drawn beside it.
That the sampling rate (or Nyquist limit) is stated whenever a spectrum is shown.
That the error axis is logarithmic when a degree or step sweep is shown.
That poles are marked together with the region of convergence.

terms.meaning: exp(tA) is the flow map of the linear ODE y' = Ay over time t.
A matrix whose eigenvectors are not orthogonal. Its norm can grow transiently though every eigenvalue decays.
w = (az + b)/(cz + d). It maps circles and lines to circles and lines and keeps angles.
Large oscillation of high-degree polynomial interpolation on equally spaced nodes near the ends of the interval.
A frequency above the Nyquist limit appears at a lower frequency after sampling.
A value of s at which a transfer function blows up; the real part decides decay or growth.
The set of s for which the Laplace integral exists; here a half-plane to the right of the rightmost pole.

remember: Eigenvalues give the long-time rate of exp(tA); the norm governs the short-time behaviour.
A Mobius map has 4 complex parameters up to scale, is invertible when ad - bc is not zero, and is conformal.
Interpolation error is a derivative term times a node polynomial: Chebyshev nodes make the node polynomial smallest.
Sampling at fs hides every frequency above fs/2 under a lower one.
For a stable linear system all poles have negative real part.

steps.title: Transient growth of a non-normal matrix
steps.note: Illustrative matrix, not the one in the figure. The off-diagonal term 5t grows linearly while e^(-t) decays: the product peaks near t = 1 before the eigenvalue bound takes over.

steps.title: Derivative of a Mobius map
steps.note: Conformal wherever the denominator is finite. The tiny residuals in the title show that the numerical map obeys the Cauchy-Riemann equations to round-off.

steps.title: Interpolation error and node choice
steps.note: The node product is huge near the ends for equispaced nodes and smallest for Chebyshev nodes. Hence the two curves of the error-against-degree panel run apart.

steps.title: Where the alias lands
steps.tex: f_\mathrm{alias}=\lvert f-k f_s\rvert,\quad f_s=32\ \text{Hz},\ f=17\ \text{Hz},\ k=1\;\Rightarrow\;15\ \text{Hz}
steps.note: Nyquist is 16 Hz here, so 17 Hz folds around it to 15 Hz. The red samples fit both waves, and the DFT peak sits in bin 15.

steps.title: Poles of a second-order response
steps.note: The real part -zeta times omega_n fixes decay, the imaginary part the ringing. With zeta = 0.92 and a real part of -1.83 the natural frequency is about 2 (computed); the imaginary part is then about 0.78, which matches the crosses.

steps.title: A nilpotent shear grows linearly
steps.note: Both eigenvalues are zero, yet the first component grows without bound: eigenvalues control exponential rates only, not polynomial growth. The companion figure plots exactly this line.

steps.title: Where the alias of 21 Hz lands
steps.note: Companion to the 17 Hz example: any frequency above 16 Hz folds back; 21 Hz and 11 Hz coincide at the sample times.

worked.title: Peak of the illustrative transient
worked.problem: For e^{tA} = e^{-t}[[1, 5t],[0, 1]] compute the 2-norm at t = 1.

solution.text: The matrix at t = 1 is e^{-1} times M = [[1,5],[0,1]]. The norm is the largest singular value.

worked.answer: About 1.9, although both eigenvalues equal -1 and the eigenvalue bound exp(-1) is 0.37: a fivefold difference.

analyze.q: All three eigenvalues of a matrix are negative and yet the norm curve rises. Does the ODE y' = Ay decay? Over which time scale would you trust the eigenvalues?
Explain how the same dots can lie on both the 17 Hz and the 15 Hz wave. What two things could you change to separate them?
analyze.hint: Sampling rate or an anti-alias filter.

analyze.q: Interpolation error is shown against degree on a log axis for two node sets. What would you expect for a function with a pole near the interval?
analyze.hint: Convergence rate depends on how far singularities are.

evaluate.q: Is it enough to report the largest eigenvalue of a learned linear map as a stability certificate? What would you add?
A student fits a degree-32 polynomial to equispaced data and reports a tiny training error. Evaluate the claim.
evaluate.hint: Training error at the nodes versus error between them.

create: Design a 2 by 2 matrix whose eigenvalues are -1 and -2 but whose norm peaks above 10, and verify with the code.
Create a title line for the aliasing figure that makes the Nyquist limit and the alias frequency impossible to miss.

checks.q: What does a Mobius map keep, and what may it change?
checks.answer: It keeps angles and maps circles and lines to circles and lines; it changes lengths and areas, and may turn a line into a circle.

checks.q: Sampled at 20 Hz, where does a 13 Hz sinusoid appear?
Why is the DFT peak of the 17 Hz wave in bin 15?
checks.hint: Which frequencies can a 32 Hz sampling distinguish?
checks.answer: Sampling at 32 Hz represents only frequencies up to 16 Hz; 17 Hz folds about 16 Hz to 15 Hz, and the DFT only sees the folded value.

checks.q: Both curves in the Runge figure interpolate exactly at their nodes. Why is one of them useless at degree 32?
checks.answer: Equispaced nodes give a node product that is huge near the ends; the error between nodes is enormous (5.1e+03 in the title) while it stays small at the nodes themselves.

checks.q: How would you display a pole-zero map so that a reader sees decay rate and ringing at once?
checks.hint: Use the geometry of the s-plane.
checks.answer: Draw lines of constant zeta and constant omega_n over the s-plane, mark poles, and print the corresponding step response beside it.
